{{< include _copilot-disclaimer.qmd >}}

This book is a style guide for writing in science, technology,
engineering, and mathematics (STEM).
Its examples come mostly from statistics and data analysis,
because that is the field I work in,
but its rules apply to any writing that explains technical ideas.

## What the book covers

The rules apply to every kind of technical document,
including:

- research papers, theses, and grant proposals;
- lecture notes, slides, and problem sets;
- reports and analysis write-ups for collaborators;
- software documentation, README files, and code comments; and
- issues, pull requests, and other messages to coauthors.

Most chapters give rules that hold for all of these documents.
Two chapters cover one kind of document each:
[Preparing a manuscript for submission](manuscript-submission.qmd)
covers journal papers,
and [Writing for teaching](teaching.qmd)
covers course materials.

## Who the book is for

I wrote this book for three groups of readers:

- students and mentees who are learning to write about their research;
- coauthors who want to know what I will ask them to change in a draft; and
- AI writing assistants that draft or edit prose for me
  or for people in my lab.

The third group is why many rules are stated as checks
that a reader can apply to a single sentence.
For example,
[Demonstrative pronouns](grammar.qmd#demonstrative-pronouns)
asks whether each "this" or "that" is followed by the noun it refers to.
A person or a program can answer that question
without knowing what the paper is about.

## How the book is organized

The chapters move from single words and terms,
to sentences,
to whole documents:

- [Defining terms clearly](defining-terms.qmd):
  how to state a definition and pair it with examples.
- [Mathematical notation](notation.qmd):
  how to write formulas that read as part of the prose.
- [Citations and evidence](citations-evidence.qmd):
  how to support each claim with a source or with data.
- [Paper organization](paper-organization.qmd):
  how to order the sections, figures, and tables of a paper.
- [Preparing a manuscript for submission](manuscript-submission.qmd):
  what journals expect of a manuscript.
- [Word choice](word-choice.qmd):
  plain words over Latin-derived ones, and concrete words over vague ones.
- [Writing for every reader](inclusive-writing.qmd):
  how to write for readers who are learning English or are neurodiverse.
- [Avoiding AI tells](avoid-ai-tells.qmd):
  the words and sentence shapes that mark machine-drafted prose.
- [Grammar](grammar.qmd):
  pronouns and sentence structures that make readers backtrack.
- [Conciseness](conciseness.qmd):
  how to say the same thing in fewer words.
- [Writing for teaching](teaching.qmd):
  the extra rules for course materials.

The [Summary](summary.qmd) lists the main rule of each section
as a checklist for revising a draft.

## How to read the book

You do not need to read the chapters in order.
Most sections state one rule,
give the reason for the rule,
and show the rule applied.
Many compare a weaker version of a passage
with a stronger one.
For example,
the [Word choice](word-choice.qmd) chapter
recommends "before" over "prior to":

> **Poor:** Prior to fitting the model, we removed outliers.
>
> **Better:** Before fitting the model, we removed outliers.

Definitions, examples, and exercises appear in numbered, colored boxes,
so that other sections and other documents can link to them.

Use the book as a reference while you write,
and use the [Summary](summary.qmd) checklist when you revise.

## Contributing

The book is a work in progress.
If a rule is unclear, wrong, or missing,
open an issue on the book's
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/psw/issues).
